title.value: Geometry and Structure of Normal Faults Forming the Eastern Boundary of Fucino Basin, Central Italy

note.value:
Normal faults present along the eastern side of the Fucino Plain, central Italy, are the object of this study. Faults juxtapose young continental sediments against massive carbonates, and are thought to control the subsurface flow of CO2-enriched groundwater. Three major normal faults are present in the area. These faults controlled the evolution of the half-graben Fucino basin, and are characterized by 0.8 km offset. The largest amount of slip occurs in the central portion of the individual faults, and it rapidly decreases towards zero at the fault tips. This slip distribution is also observed in the wide dextral overstep between two adjacent major faults. This step is characterized by two sets of NW-trending normal faults that form NW-elongated structural depressions.

Faults in the study area formed parallel to one of the two main sets of solution surfaces present in the host rock. Major normal faults are segmented into minor fault panels. Kinematic markers present along normal faults, striations and slickenfibers, show the occurrence of minor components of left- lateral slip. Within the quarries excavating the carbonate fault footwalls, three main zones of damaged rocks flank the fault core. Fault rocks closer to the fault core are more deformed then fault rocks farther away from it. The fault core is composed by meter thick fault gouge and matrix- supported cataclasites. Thin horizon of cemented fault rocks formed in the vicinity of the hanging wall- footwall contact. Sediments on the hanging wall are widely deformed by faults with centimeter to decimeter offset, and locally drape the fault planes.

Laboratory analyses have been performed on two core plugs of damaged host rock and matrix- supported cataclasite collected in the study area. The fault rock formed by intense fragmentation and comminution of the limestone host rock, which caused the original limestone porosity of 13.8% to decrease down to 0.8%. Mineralogical analysis of these rock samples is consistent with the host rock being composed of platform-related boundstones with dark and minute lime-mud filling the pore- space. The matrix-supported cataclasite comprises angular-to-subrounded clasts in fine calcite matrix. Occasionally, low-Mg calcite cement is present in the fault rock either within fractures or as meniscus cement. After rock physics experiments, the elastic moduli of both samples of damaged limestone and fault rock do not sensitively change with increasing confining pressure. Both samples show almost linear elastic behavior, and do not exhibit any hysteresis during cycles of confining pressure. Vp increases during the first steps of pressure increments, and then it remains constant. The increase occurs more rapidly in the matrix-supported rock then in the damaged host rock. Vs is almost constant during the whole cycle of pressure. These velocity trends suggest the presence of more rounded, less flat, micro-pores in the fault rock relative to the damaged limestone host rock. Small variations of Vp/Vs ratio with pressure are observed in the limestone rock sample, and indicate the closure of small cracks within the damaged host rock. Overall, these velocity data show small textural differences between the two study samples. Since their different texture is recognized under the optical microscope (massive, cracked limestone host rock vs. granular, matrix- supported fault rock), this similarity is due to the presence of meniscus cement in the fault rock. This cement binds clasts of the granular rock all together, and makes the whole rock stiffer and much rigid.

Agosta, Fabrizio. (2003). Geometry and Structure of Normal Faults Forming the Eastern Boundary of Fucino Basin, Central Italy. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: http://purl.stanford.edu/jn231mr1766
